text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

S-E-Banken's chief economist Klas Eklund believes the government of Goran Persson is losing its grip on economic policy, according to a circular he is sending to bank customers today. Instead of further steps towards stability there is now toing and froing, a step back, then back to square one, Eklund said. Persson may well survive today's vote of no-confidence in parliament, but it is not his handling of China policy which is threatening to undermine confidence in this government by the international capital markets.

-Swedes are squirrelling away medicines worth about 500 million crowns, fearing that they will become dearer in the new year. On November 27, parliament will vote on a bill which would require each patient to pay 1,300 crowns in a 12-month period for prescribed medicines and contraceptive pills. In addition, long-term illness treatments which had previously been exempt will now be included.

-Practically all fish-farming could be outlawed in Sweden if the nature protection agency succeeds in pushing through tough new policy affecting gene technology and the establishment of non-indigenous animals and living organisms. The proposal is doing the rounds of relevant authorities and has caused surprise and some alarm.

-The Swedish employers' federation SAF wants tougher rules on settling industrial conflict, including obligatory union referenda before strikes and lockouts and the outlawing of secondary picketing, and improved mediation services. The federation maintains that, despite high unemployment, wages are being driven unrealistically high by workplace conflicts or the threat of them.

-A seminar for members and analysts at the Stockholm bourse arrived at no firm conclusions on what constituted privileged information, the paper's stocks correspondent wrote. The bourse officials expressed alarm at what has been called "massaging analysts," whereby companies give information to a group of experts but not to the press and public. "Like other forms of massage, it can be more or less decent," the paper wrote.

-Swedes are getting fatter, according to new surveys, one of which shows that the number of overweight young men has doubled since the 1970s and that 15-year-olds today have put on three to four kilograms on average compared with their elder siblings 10 years ago. A reduction in the number of hours devoted to physical training in schools is being blamed as one of the causes.

-Lower state housing subsidies and much higher property taxes will cause a new wave of mortgage defaults over the next two years. State-owned credit company Venantius says its portfolio consists of high-risk mortgages. "Our calculations suggest that cooperatively owned apartments and private homeowners will have big problems in both 1997 and 1998," Venantius president Eva-Britt Gustafsson said.

-State-owned Telia, Sweden's largest and state-owned telephone company, is in advanced talks with Danish television and film company Egmont about cooperation, according to the Danish daily Politiken. Telia is lobbying hard to obtain approval from Swedish political leaders for an aggressive programme into multimedia fields, using telephony as the foundation.

-After Norway, Sweden and Finland, Australia is the country with the greatest per capita use of mobile telephones. When an Australian lifts a cellular phone to his ear to make a call, it's 96 percent likely to be through Ericsson switchgear. The Swedish company's sales have doubled in the last three years and the subsidiary firm won the coveted Australian Quality Award.
